title: Leftmost Value on the Deepest Level
statement:
You get the root of a non-empty binary tree. Look at its deepest level, the one farthest from the root. Return the value of the node that sits furthest to the left on that level.

"Furthest left" means first when the level is read from left to right. That node is not always a left child, and it is not always under the root's left subtree.

examples.why: The deepest level holds only 5, under the root's right side. Walking down left children would stop at 9.
The root alone is the deepest level.
The deepest level reads 4, 5. The 4 is a right child, but it still comes first.

hints: Reading a tree level by level is breadth-first search. Which node of the last level does BFS see first?
With BFS, remember the first node of every level; the last one you remember is the answer.

A neat variant: enqueue the right child before the left one. Then the very last node dequeued is the leftmost node of the deepest level. A DFS also works if it visits left before right and records a value only when it first reaches a new depth.

explain.intuition:
The question is about levels, so read the tree level by level with a queue, like walking a DOM tree breadth-first. The first node taken out on each level is that level's leftmost node, and the last level processed is the deepest. Keep overwriting the answer with each level's first node.

A shorter trick: push the right child before the left. Then every level is read from right to left, and the very last node to leave the queue is the leftmost node of the bottom level. DFS works too: go left before right and record a value only the first time you reach a new depth; the first node reached at any depth is that depth's leftmost.
steps: Put the root in a queue.
While the queue is not empty, take the next node and store its value as the current answer.
Push its right child, then its left child (skipping missing ones).
When the queue empties, the stored value is the leftmost node of the deepest level.
pitfalls: Following left children only. The deepest level may hang off a right branch (example 1).
Returning a left child instead of the leftmost node. In example 3 the answer is a right child.
In DFS, overwriting the answer whenever depth is at least the best so far (≥ instead of >), which returns the rightmost node.

complexity.space: O(w) for the widest level (BFS) or O(h) for the height (DFS)

solutions.title: BFS, right child first
solutions.idea: Read each level from right to left; the last node dequeued is the bottom-left one.

solutions.title: DFS, first node at each new depth
solutions.idea: Visit left before right. The first node to reach a depth deeper than any seen so far is the leftmost at that depth.

followups: Return the leftmost value of every level, top to bottom. How does that relate to the view of the tree from the left side?
Return the rightmost value of the deepest level instead. Which one line changes in each solution?
